newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street awaits PPI data, seen firm at open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street awaits PPI data, seen firm at open.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open steady to modestly higher Friday, taking some early direction from the Producer Price Index for June but also buoyed by yesterday's rebound.
As long as PPI, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, does not show any evidence of inflation, share prices are set to rise at the opening, analysts said.

"We have some carry-through momentum from yesterday and stocks are higher in Europe," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "Provided the PPI is copacetic, I look for another decent open."

He said shares of long-distance telephone companies are likely to feel pressure after MCI Communications Corp forecast that its earnings for the 1997 second half and into 1998 would fall below Wall Street expectations due to delays in gaining entry into U.S. local phone service markets.
"This could hit AT&T and Sprint," Wachtel said.
The broader market will focus on PPI and second quarter earnings reports, analysts said.
PPI is expected to be unchanged, compared with a 0.3 percent decline in May. The core rate, excluding food and energy prices, is seen up 0.1 percent, compared with a decline of 0.3 percent in May.
If the index shows a jump in prices, inflation-wary bonds could stumble, with stocks following suit, analysts said.
"If the PPI shows clear-cut evidence of higher prices, it could bring the Fed back into the picture..." said Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics.
Ahead of the data, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index rose 0.30 point to 921.80, while the long bond was up 4/32 at a 6.56 percent yield.
On Thursday the Dow Jones Industrial Average recouped early losses to close up 44.33 points at 7886.76, helped by solid earnings reports from several of its components.

Among today's earnings reports, Chrysler Corp posted second quarter earnings of $0.70 per share -- including $438 million lost because of a strike -- compared to $1.38 in the year-ago quarter and a First Call estimate of $0.68.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that investors have made handsome profits by betting on the once-weak bonds of Italy and Spain, in anticipation of a single European currency.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that mutual funds that invest in equities added $18 billion in new cash in June, according to a trade group estimate.
